### Composition of the CRSP Sample {#sec-bem7-composition}

Figures 7.1–7.4 of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016) decompose the sample by
exchange and industry from December 1925 to December 2012. Count every
stock in the month-end universe, even if market capitalization is
missing. For market value, sum only observed capitalization. Convert
nominal millions to billions of December 2012 dollars using the ratio
of December 2012 CPI to that month's CPI.

#### Stock Exchange Composition of CRSP Sample {#exchanges .unnumbered .unlisted}

The book groups exchange codes 1 and 31 as NYSE, 2 and 32 as AMEX, and
3 and 33 as Nasdaq. All remaining codes go into *Other*.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

exchange = (
    pl.when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([1, 31])).then(pl.lit("NYSE"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([2, 32])).then(pl.lit("AMEX"))
    .when(pl.col("exchcd").is_in([3, 33])).then(pl.lit("Nasdaq"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("Other"))
)

composition = (
    universe
    .filter(pl.col("month").is_between(pl.date(1925, 12, 1), pl.date(2012, 12, 1)))
    .select("month", "cap", "siccd", exchange=exchange)
    .join(cpi.lazy(), on="month", how="left", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(real_cap=pl.col("cap") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi") / 1000)
    .collect()
)

assert composition["cpi"].is_not_null().all()
assert composition["cpi"].gt(0).all()
assert composition["month"].n_unique() == 1045

def summarize_composition(sample, group, labels):
    summary = sample.group_by("month", group).agg(
        stocks=pl.len(),
        value=pl.col("real_cap").sum(),
    )
    grid = sample.select("month").unique().join(
        pl.DataFrame({group: labels}), how="cross"
    )
    return (
        grid
        .join(summary, on=["month", group], how="left", validate="1:1")
        .with_columns(pl.col("stocks", "value").fill_null(0))
        .sort("month")
    )

exchange_labels = ["NYSE", "AMEX", "Nasdaq", "Other"]
by_exchange = summarize_composition(composition, "exchange", exchange_labels)
total = (
    by_exchange
    .group_by("month")
    .agg(pl.col("stocks", "value").sum())
    .with_columns(exchange=pl.lit("Total"))
    .select(by_exchange.columns)
)
by_exchange = pl.concat([total, by_exchange])

def plot_composition(data, group, labels, measure, y_label):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4), layout="constrained")
    colors = plt.get_cmap("tab20").colors
    for label, color in zip(labels, colors[::2] + colors[1::2]):
        series = data.filter(pl.col(group) == label).sort("month")
        ax.plot(series["month"], series[measure], label=label,
                color="black" if label == "Total" else color)
    ax.set(xlabel="Month", ylabel=y_label, ylim=(0, None))
    ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.2)
    ax.legend(ncol=3, frameon=False)
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem7-exchange-count
#| fig-cap: "Number of stocks by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.1."
#| fig-alt: "Stock counts jump when AMEX and Nasdaq stocks enter the sample. Total count peaks in the late 1990s."

plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "stocks", "Number of stocks");
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem7-exchange-value
#| fig-cap: "Market value by exchange, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.2."
#| fig-alt: "The NYSE accounts for most of the sample market value. Nasdaq grows considerably in the late 1990s."

plot_composition(by_exchange, "exchange", ["Total", *exchange_labels],
                 "value", "Market value ($ billions, December 2012)");
```

AMEX enters the data in July 1962. Most Nasdaq coverage starts in December
1972. The value series jumps much less than the count series at those dates:
market coverage can change substantially without much change in market value.
Keep that distinction in mind when comparing equal- and value-weighted results
across time.

The following checkpoints compare the reconstructed exchange counts with
the figures quoted in the book's text. The authors report a December 2012
total of 3,675, but their four exchange counts add up to 3,677. Keep both
benchmarks rather than forcing the component counts to match the printed
total. The available legacy CRSP file is a later vintage; the count
differences do not by themselves identify revisions or coding differences.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem7-count-checkpoints
#| tbl-cap: "Exchange-count checkpoints reported by BEM and reconstructed from the available CRSP vintage."

benchmarks = pl.DataFrame({
    "checkpoint": ["1925-12", "1962-06", "1962-07", "1972-11",
                   "1972-12", "1997-11", "2012-12"],
    "printed_total": [499, 1130, 1963, 2666, 5534, 7544, 3675],
    "printed_nyse": [499, 1121, 1125, 1378, 1386, 1862, 1319],
    "printed_amex": [0, 0, 834, 1133, 1135, 572, 226],
    "printed_nasdaq": [0, 0, 0, 102, 2896, 5029, 2130],
    "printed_other": [0, 9, 4, 53, 117, 81, 2],
})
actual_counts = (
    by_exchange
    .with_columns(checkpoint=pl.col("month").dt.strftime("%Y-%m"))
    .pivot(on="exchange", index="checkpoint", values="stocks")
)
count_checkpoints = (
    benchmarks
    .join(actual_counts, on="checkpoint", validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(total_difference=pl.col("Total") - pl.col("printed_total"))
)

count_checkpoints.select(
    "checkpoint", "printed_total", reconstructed_total="Total",
    difference="total_difference",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem7-exchange-end
#| tbl-cap: "Exchange counts at the end of 2012."

last_counts = count_checkpoints.filter(pl.col("checkpoint") == "2012-12")
labels = ["NYSE", "AMEX", "Nasdaq", "Other", "Total"]
pl.DataFrame({
    "exchange": labels,
    "printed": [last_counts[f"printed_{label.lower()}"].item() for label in labels],
    "reconstructed": [last_counts[label].item() for label in labels],
})
```

The local December 2012 universe has 3,742 common stocks. Of the 86 in
the Other category, 85 have no usable capitalization in this vintage.
That helps explain why a visible difference in counts need not produce
a comparable difference in market value, but does not tell us why the
book counted only two Other stocks.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem7-value-checkpoints
#| tbl-cap: "Market-value checkpoints in billions of December 2012 dollars; the book values are approximate."

value_benchmarks = pl.DataFrame({
    "checkpoint": ["1925-12", "1972-12", "2000-03", "2012-12"],
    "printed_billions": [341, 5300, 22500, 15700],
})
reconstructed = (
    total
    .select(checkpoint=pl.col("month").dt.strftime("%Y-%m"),
            reconstructed_billions=pl.col("value").round(1))
)
(
    value_benchmarks
    .join(reconstructed, on="checkpoint", validate="1:1")
    .with_columns(difference_billions=(
        pl.col("reconstructed_billions") - pl.col("printed_billions")
    ).round(1))
)
```

The reconstructed market value is about $15.72 trillion in December
2012, close to the book's $15.7 trillion despite the difference in
stock counts.

#### Industry Composition of CRSP Sample {#industries .unnumbered .unlisted}

We use the security's current SIC code rather than a code carried back
from a later date. [OSHA's SIC manual](https://www.osha.gov/data/sic-manual)
describes the divisions. The table uses the intervals in BEM Table 7.1,
with shortened labels. Keep zero and null codes separate from nonmissing
codes that do not fall in a listed interval.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem7-sic
#| tbl-cap: "SIC code ranges used in the industry breakdown (BEM Table 7.1)."

sic_divisions = pl.DataFrame({
    "first_sic": [1, 1000, 1500, 2000, 4000, 5000, 5200, 6000, 7000, 9000],
    "last_sic": [999, 1499, 1799, 3999, 4999, 5199, 5999, 6799, 8999, 9999],
    "industry": ["Agriculture", "Mining", "Construction", "Manufacturing",
                 "Transport and utilities", "Wholesale", "Retail",
                 "Finance", "Services", "Public administration"],
})
with pl.Config(tbl_rows=12):
    display(sic_divisions)
```

```{python}
industry = pl.coalesce([
    pl.when(pl.col("siccd").is_between(lo, hi)).then(pl.lit(name))
    for lo, hi, name in sic_divisions.iter_rows()
])
classified = composition.with_columns(
    industry=pl.when(pl.col("siccd").fill_null(0) == 0).then(pl.lit("Missing"))
    .otherwise(industry.fill_null("Unclassified"))
)
industry_labels = [*sic_divisions["industry"].to_list(), "Missing"]
if classified["industry"].eq("Unclassified").any():
    industry_labels.append("Unclassified")
by_industry = summarize_composition(classified, "industry", industry_labels)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem7-industry-count
#| fig-cap: "Number of stocks by SIC division, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.3."
#| fig-alt: "Manufacturing is the largest industry by stock count, with sharp changes in several industries when Nasdaq enters."

plot_composition(by_industry, "industry", industry_labels,
                 "stocks", "Number of stocks");
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem7-industry-value
#| fig-cap: "Market value by SIC division, recreating the series in BEM Figure 7.4."
#| fig-alt: "Manufacturing has the largest market value. Communications, grouped with transport and utilities, and services grow during the dot-com boom."

plot_composition(by_industry, "industry", industry_labels,
                 "value", "Market value ($ billions, December 2012)");
```
